text: High Blood Pressure
explanation_or_correction: TBD: guideline (to be chosen with Dr. Abbas, e.g. Hypertension Canada)

text: What blood pressure numbers mean: The top (systolic) and bottom (diastolic) numbers, what each measures, the unit (mmHg), and why a single reading can differ from a person's usual blood pressure.
A blood pressure reading is written as two numbers, one over the other. What does the top number measure?
option_A: The amount of blood in the body
option_B: The number of heartbeats per minute
option_C: The pressure in the arteries while the heart beats and pumps blood
option_D: The pressure in the arteries while the heart rests between beats
explanation_or_correction: The top (systolic) number is the pressure while the heart contracts; the bottom (diastolic) number is the pressure while it rests between beats.

text: What does the bottom (diastolic) number of a blood pressure reading measure?
option_A: The pressure in the arteries while the heart rests between beats
option_B: How fast blood flows through the body
option_C: The pressure while the heart has stopped
option_D: The pressure inside the veins
explanation_or_correction: The heart does not stop between beats; it relaxes and refills. The diastolic number is the arterial pressure during that pause.

text: Why is high blood pressure often called a 'silent' condition?
option_A: It can only be measured while a person sleeps
option_B: It only matters in older adults
option_C: It often causes no noticeable symptoms
option_D: It always causes headaches that people tend to ignore
explanation_or_correction: Many people with high blood pressure feel completely well, so regular measurement is the only way to know.

text: A person's top number is usually in the normal range, but their bottom number is repeatedly raised. Which general statement is most accurate?
option_A: It does not matter, because only the top number counts
option_B: It proves that the blood pressure monitor is broken
option_C: It means the heart stops for too long between beats
option_D: A raised bottom number can still be a concern and is worth discussing with a clinician
explanation_or_correction: Both numbers are used to judge blood pressure; either one can be raised.

text: High blood pressure always causes symptoms such as headaches.
explanation_or_correction: High blood pressure often causes no symptoms at all, which is why regular measurement matters. Feeling well does not show that blood pressure is normal.

text: Only the top number of a blood pressure reading matters.
explanation_or_correction: Both numbers matter. Either the top (systolic) or the bottom (diastolic) number can be raised, and both are used to judge blood pressure.

text: The bottom number is the pressure when the heart stops.
explanation_or_correction: The heart does not stop between beats; it relaxes and refills. The bottom (diastolic) number is the pressure in the arteries while the heart rests between beats.

text: How high blood pressure is classified and diagnosed: Diagnosis is based on several readings over time, sometimes with home or 24-hour monitoring; readings are grouped into categories whose cut-offs depend on the guideline; how to measure correctly.
How is high blood pressure usually confirmed?
option_A: From whether the person has headaches
option_B: From a blood test alone
option_C: From a single reading at one visit
option_D: From several readings taken on different occasions
explanation_or_correction: Blood pressure varies, so a diagnosis is based on repeated readings over time, sometimes including home or 24-hour monitoring.

text: Which of these helps get an accurate blood pressure reading at home?
option_A: Measuring right after climbing stairs or drinking coffee
option_B: Sitting quietly for a few minutes with the back supported, feet flat and the arm resting at heart level
option_C: Measuring over thick clothing while talking
option_D: Measuring only when you feel a headache
explanation_or_correction: Rest, a supported back and arm, feet flat, the cuff on a bare arm and no talking all help the reading reflect usual blood pressure.

text: Why might a clinician suggest home or 24-hour (ambulatory) blood pressure monitoring?
option_A: To see blood pressure over time and outside the clinic, for example when clinic readings may be higher than usual
option_B: As a formality, because home readings cannot be trusted
option_C: Because one clinic reading is always enough to decide
option_D: To measure cholesterol
explanation_or_correction: Some people's readings are higher in the clinic than in daily life; readings over time give a fuller picture.

text: Why do clinicians group readings into categories such as 'normal', 'elevated' and 'high'?
option_A: Because the cut-offs are the same in every country and never change
option_B: Because the categories describe how a person feels
option_C: To guide follow-up and treatment decisions; the exact cut-offs depend on the guideline being followed
option_D: Because any reading above normal means medicine must be started immediately
explanation_or_correction: Categories support decisions about checks, lifestyle and treatment. Guidelines differ in their exact numbers, so this course states which guideline it follows.

text: One high reading means a person has high blood pressure.
explanation_or_correction: Blood pressure changes during the day, for example with activity, stress or caffeine. High blood pressure is diagnosed from several readings taken on different occasions, sometimes with home or 24-hour monitoring.

text: Home blood pressure readings are not useful; only clinic readings count.
explanation_or_correction: Home readings taken with a validated device and the right technique give useful information over time, and clinicians often use them, for example when clinic readings may be higher than usual.

text: Risk factors and causes: Factors that raise the risk, such as a high-salt diet, low physical activity, excess weight, heavy alcohol use, older age and family history; which of them can and cannot be changed.
Which of these is a common risk factor for high blood pressure?
option_A: Sleeping on the left side
option_B: Eating fruit every day
option_C: Drinking water regularly
option_D: A diet high in salt (sodium)
explanation_or_correction: A high-salt diet is one of the best-known risk factors; others include low activity, excess weight, heavy alcohol use, age and family history.

text: Which statement about age and high blood pressure is correct?
option_A: Only people over 60 can have high blood pressure
option_B: Blood pressure always falls as people get older
option_C: The risk rises with age, but younger adults can also have high blood pressure
option_D: Age has nothing to do with blood pressure
explanation_or_correction: Age is a risk factor, but high blood pressure is not limited to older people.

text: Which risk factor for high blood pressure cannot be changed by lifestyle?
option_A: Alcohol use
option_B: Salt intake
option_C: Family history
option_D: Physical activity
explanation_or_correction: Family history and age cannot be changed; diet, activity, weight and alcohol can.

text: Why can someone who feels well and is not stressed still have high blood pressure?
option_A: Because stress is the only cause, so they must be stressed without knowing it
option_B: Because long-term factors such as family history, diet and weight also raise blood pressure, and it usually causes no symptoms
option_C: Because high blood pressure is caused only by old age
option_D: They cannot: feeling well shows that blood pressure is normal
explanation_or_correction: High blood pressure has many contributing factors and is often silent, so how a person feels says little about it.

text: Only older people get high blood pressure.
explanation_or_correction: The risk rises with age, but younger adults and sometimes children can also have high blood pressure.

text: High blood pressure is caused only by stress.
explanation_or_correction: Stress can raise blood pressure for a while, but long-term high blood pressure has many contributing factors, such as diet, physical activity, body weight, alcohol, family history and other health conditions.

text: Why it matters (heart, brain, kidney and eye complications): Long-term high blood pressure strains the heart and damages blood vessels, raising the risk of heart attack, stroke, kidney disease and eye problems, often without symptoms.
Over many years, untreated high blood pressure raises the risk of which problems?
option_A: The common cold
option_B: Sunburn
option_C: Heart problems only, and nothing else
option_D: Heart attack, stroke and kidney disease
explanation_or_correction: High pressure damages blood vessels throughout the body, including those of the heart, brain and kidneys.

text: How does long-term high blood pressure harm the body?
option_A: It thickens the blood within a single day
option_B: It makes the heart work harder and damages blood vessels over time
option_C: It affects the heart but no other organ
option_D: It only harms people who notice symptoms
explanation_or_correction: The extra pressure strains the heart and gradually damages artery walls, which affects many organs.

text: Why do regular blood pressure checks matter even when a person feels fine?
option_A: They do not matter as long as the person feels fine
option_B: Because the check itself lowers blood pressure
option_C: High blood pressure often has no symptoms but can still cause damage
option_D: Because headaches always come first and warn the person
explanation_or_correction: Because the condition is often silent, measuring is the only way to find it early.

text: Which organs can be affected by long-term high blood pressure?
option_A: Only the skin
option_B: Only the heart
option_C: Only the lungs
option_D: The heart, brain, kidneys and eyes
explanation_or_correction: Damage to blood vessels can lead to heart disease, stroke, kidney disease and changes in the eyes.

text: High blood pressure only affects the heart.
explanation_or_correction: Long-term high blood pressure can also damage the blood vessels of the brain, kidneys and eyes, raising the risk of stroke, kidney disease and vision problems.

text: Lifestyle management (salt, diet, activity, alcohol, weight): Everyday changes that help lower blood pressure, where most dietary salt comes from, and how lifestyle changes work alongside medicine.
Which change can help lower blood pressure?
option_A: Drinking more alcohol
option_B: Sitting for longer each day
option_C: Adding more salt to meals
option_D: Eating less salt
explanation_or_correction: Reducing salt is one of the most effective dietary changes for blood pressure.

text: Where does most of the salt (sodium) in a typical diet come from?
option_A: The salt shaker at the table
option_B: Fresh fruit
option_C: Drinking water
option_D: Processed, packaged and restaurant foods
explanation_or_correction: Most sodium is already in foods before they reach the table, so reading labels and cooking at home help.

text: Which combination is generally recommended to help manage blood pressure?
option_A: Avoiding all physical activity
option_B: Regular physical activity, a diet rich in vegetables, fruit and whole grains, limiting alcohol and keeping a healthy weight
option_C: Only leaving out table salt, with no other change
option_D: No change, because nothing helps once blood pressure is high
explanation_or_correction: Several everyday changes together have the largest effect.

text: A person already takes blood pressure medicine. Which statement about lifestyle changes is most accurate?
option_A: They only matter for older people
option_B: They can still help and work alongside the medicine; any change to the medicine is discussed with a clinician
option_C: They no longer make any difference
option_D: They mean the medicine can be stopped right away
explanation_or_correction: Lifestyle changes and medicine complement each other; decisions about medicine are made with a clinician.

text: Not using the salt shaker is enough to eat little salt.
explanation_or_correction: Most salt (sodium) in a typical diet comes from processed, packaged and restaurant foods, not from the salt shaker. Reading food labels helps.

text: Once blood pressure is high, lifestyle changes no longer help.
explanation_or_correction: Lifestyle changes can lower blood pressure at any stage, and they work alongside medicine when medicine is needed.

text: Medication and adherence (general principles only): Why blood pressure medicines are taken regularly as prescribed, why normal readings on treatment do not mean stopping, and why side effects or changes are discussed with a clinician. No drug names or doses.
A person's blood pressure has been normal for three months while taking medication. What is generally recommended?
option_A: Take half of it from now on without asking anyone
option_B: Take it only on days with headaches
option_C: Keep taking it, and discuss any change with their doctor
option_D: Stop the medication, because blood pressure is now normal
explanation_or_correction: Normal readings on treatment usually mean the medicine is working. Changes are decided with a clinician.

text: Why is it important to take blood pressure medicine regularly, as prescribed?
option_A: It keeps blood pressure controlled over time, and high blood pressure usually cannot be felt
option_B: Because a person can feel when their pressure rises and take it only then
option_C: It is only needed on days with symptoms
option_D: Because one dose cures high blood pressure permanently
explanation_or_correction: Blood pressure medicines work while they are taken regularly; symptoms are not a reliable guide.

text: Why might a clinician prescribe more than one blood pressure medicine for some people?
option_A: Because all blood pressure medicines work in exactly the same way
option_B: Because the first medicine always fails
option_C: So that lifestyle changes are no longer needed
option_D: Different medicines work in different ways and can be combined to control blood pressure
explanation_or_correction: Combining medicines with different actions is a common way to reach control; lifestyle changes still help.

text: Someone notices a possible side effect from their blood pressure medicine. What is the safest general step?
option_A: Contact a doctor, nurse or pharmacist to discuss it rather than stopping on their own
option_B: Take a double dose to make up for it
option_C: Stop the medicine immediately without telling anyone
option_D: Switch to a family member's medicine
explanation_or_correction: A clinician can check whether it is a side effect and adjust treatment safely.

text: Blood pressure medication can be stopped once readings are normal.
explanation_or_correction: Normal readings while taking a medicine usually show that the treatment is working. Stopping or changing it should be discussed with a clinician first.

text: Blood pressure medicine is only needed on days when you feel unwell.
explanation_or_correction: High blood pressure usually cannot be felt. Medicine keeps blood pressure controlled when it is taken regularly as prescribed, not only on days with symptoms.

text: Type 2 Diabetes
explanation_or_correction: Draft educational reference: MedlinePlus, https://medlineplus.gov/diabetestype2.html. Course-specific guideline and teaching level to be confirmed with Lavin.

text: Glucose and insulin basics: Glucose as an energy source; the role of insulin in helping glucose enter body cells.
Which statement about insulin is correct?
option_A: Insulin helps glucose move from the blood into cells
option_B: Insulin is a hormone produced by the lungs
option_C: Insulin cannot affect blood glucose
option_D: Insulin normally keeps glucose out of body cells
explanation_or_correction: Insulin helps blood glucose enter cells where it can be used for energy.

text: Where does much of the body's glucose come from?
option_A: The hair follicles
option_B: Food that is eaten
option_C: Bones alone
option_D: The air breathed in
explanation_or_correction: Glucose comes largely from the foods we eat.

text: Which description best fits high blood glucose?
option_A: The body has stopped making energy completely
option_B: All glucose has disappeared from cells
option_C: Too much glucose remains in the bloodstream
option_D: The bloodstream contains no water
explanation_or_correction: When insulin is insufficient or less effective, blood glucose may remain high.

text: Insulin normally raises blood sugar by keeping glucose out of cells.
explanation_or_correction: Insulin helps glucose enter cells and generally lowers the amount of glucose remaining in blood.

text: Insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes: Cells' reduced response to insulin, compensatory insulin production and rising blood glucose.
What is insulin resistance?
option_A: Having no blood glucose at all
option_B: A sudden infection of the pancreas
option_C: The body produces no insulin at all
option_D: Cells not responding normally to insulin
explanation_or_correction: With insulin resistance, cells do not respond to insulin as effectively.

text: What may happen when the body's insulin response becomes less effective?
option_A: The pancreas may initially make more insulin
option_B: The lungs begin making insulin
option_C: Blood glucose can never rise
option_D: Insulin is no longer a hormone
explanation_or_correction: The body may compensate by making more insulin, but blood glucose can eventually rise.

text: Which statement about type 2 diabetes is most accurate?
option_A: It always begins in childhood
option_B: It involves the body's difficulty using insulin effectively, sometimes with insufficient insulin production
option_C: It is diagnosed by counting the number of meals eaten
option_D: It is always caused by eating one sugary food
explanation_or_correction: Type 2 diabetes often involves insulin resistance and reduced ability to maintain normal glucose levels.

text: Insulin resistance means the body has no insulin at all.
explanation_or_correction: In insulin resistance, cells respond less well to insulin; the body may still produce insulin.

text: Risk factors and prevention: Family history, physical activity and other modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors.
Which statement about type 2 diabetes risk is accurate?
option_A: Only one factor can ever affect risk
option_B: Only people with a family history can develop type 2 diabetes
option_C: Family history can increase risk, but diabetes can also occur without it
option_D: Everyone has exactly the same risk
explanation_or_correction: Family history is one recognized risk factor, though it is not necessary for diabetes to develop.

text: Which is an example of a modifiable risk factor?
option_A: Family history
option_B: Inherited genes
option_C: Date of birth
option_D: Physical activity level
explanation_or_correction: Activity levels can be modified, unlike age or inherited risk.

text: Why should a person with several risk factors ask about screening?
option_A: To establish whether testing is appropriate even when symptoms are absent
option_B: Because a risk factor always means they have diabetes
option_C: Because screening replaces all follow-up care
option_D: Because they can determine diagnosis from family history alone
explanation_or_correction: Risk factors can guide a healthcare professional's decision about appropriate screening.

text: Only people with a family history can develop type 2 diabetes.
explanation_or_correction: Family history can raise risk, but it is not required for type 2 diabetes to develop.

text: Monitoring and complications: Why glucose is monitored and why long-term high blood glucose can affect organs.
Which statement about glucose monitoring is accurate?
option_A: Feeling well always means monitoring is unnecessary
option_B: Monitoring helps show glucose trends and support management discussions
option_C: Monitoring determines eye colour
option_D: One measurement replaces every clinical review
explanation_or_correction: Glucose measurements help individuals and care teams evaluate management over time.

text: Which body systems can be affected by prolonged high blood glucose?
option_A: Only the fingernails
option_B: Only the nose
option_C: Blood vessels, nerves, kidneys and eyes
option_D: No body systems
explanation_or_correction: Long-term high blood glucose can affect blood vessels, nerves and several organs.

text: Why might a clinician review a pattern of readings rather than only one number?
option_A: All readings are identical throughout the day
option_B: One high number always confirms a complication
option_C: A reading cannot be affected by daily conditions
option_D: Trends over time provide more context than an isolated measurement
explanation_or_correction: Blood glucose changes over time; patterns can help guide clinical decisions.

text: Feeling well proves that blood glucose is within the target range.
explanation_or_correction: High blood glucose can occur without noticeable symptoms; monitoring and professional guidance matter.

text: Self-management and professional follow-up: Everyday self-management, following an individualized care plan and checking treatment changes with a care team.
Which action supports safe diabetes self-management?
option_A: Following an agreed care plan and discussing changes with the care team
option_B: Taking another person's prescription
option_C: Changing medicine doses based on an online quiz
option_D: Stopping prescribed diabetes treatment as soon as symptoms improve
explanation_or_correction: Self-management includes following a personalized plan and reviewing changes with healthcare professionals.

text: Which approach is best for learning how lifestyle factors affect glucose?
option_A: Change all medicines without discussion
option_B: Record relevant patterns and discuss them with the healthcare team
option_C: Assume everyone should follow the same plan
option_D: Ignore the effect of activity
explanation_or_correction: Tracking relevant patterns can inform individualized care conversations.

text: What should a student conclude from a fictional class case where glucose is repeatedly above a prescribed target?
option_A: A diagnosis and dose can be selected from the quiz alone
option_B: The record has no educational value
option_C: The pattern should be reviewed in the context of an individualized clinical care plan
option_D: The patient should skip every meal
explanation_or_correction: A pattern should be interpreted in a clinical context; education questions do not give individual treatment directions.

text: A person should change or stop prescribed diabetes treatment as soon as symptoms improve.
explanation_or_correction: Changes to prescribed diabetes care should be discussed with the treating healthcare professional.

text: Asthma
explanation_or_correction: Draft educational reference: MedlinePlus, https://medlineplus.gov/asthma.html. Clinical assessment/treatment guidance to be confirmed by Lavin.

text: Airways and asthma basics: Chronic inflammation and narrowing of airways, and how this affects breathing.
What part of the body is mainly affected by asthma?
option_A: The outer ear
option_B: The airways carrying air to and from the lungs
option_C: The stomach rather than the airways
option_D: The stomach lining
explanation_or_correction: Asthma is a chronic condition of the airways, which can become inflamed and narrowed.

text: What may happen to the airways during asthma symptoms?
option_A: They carry blood instead of air
option_B: They become rigid bone
option_C: They become inflamed and narrower
option_D: They disappear temporarily
explanation_or_correction: Airway inflammation and narrowing can make breathing more difficult.

text: Why can asthma cause difficulty breathing?
option_A: The heart stops permanently
option_B: The body stops producing saliva
option_C: The throat turns into muscle
option_D: Airways can narrow and become inflamed
explanation_or_correction: Inflammation and narrowing of the airways can restrict airflow.

text: Asthma affects the stomach rather than the airways.
explanation_or_correction: Asthma is a long-term condition involving inflammation and narrowing of the airways.

text: Symptoms and flare-ups: Wheezing, coughing, chest tightness and shortness of breath, and recognizing worsening symptoms.
Which statement about asthma symptoms is accurate?
option_A: Asthma may cause wheezing, coughing or chest tightness
option_B: Everyone has exactly the same symptoms
option_C: Wheezing is the only symptom asthma can cause
option_D: Eye colour always changes with asthma
explanation_or_correction: Wheezing, coughing, chest tightness and shortness of breath are common asthma symptoms.

text: What is meant by an asthma flare-up?
option_A: A type of skin infection
option_B: A period when asthma symptoms become worse than usual
option_C: A routine change in hair colour
option_D: Proof that every medication has failed
explanation_or_correction: A flare-up is a worsening of asthma symptoms.

text: What should someone with rapidly worsening breathing symptoms do?
option_A: Wait for a classroom assessment
option_B: Ignore the symptoms because all asthma symptoms are harmless
option_C: Follow their written action plan and seek urgent medical help when indicated
option_D: Select a medicine dose from an online quiz
explanation_or_correction: Urgent breathing difficulty needs appropriate medical attention following the individual's action plan.

text: Wheezing is the only possible asthma symptom.
explanation_or_correction: Asthma may involve coughing, chest tightness, shortness of breath and wheezing; symptoms vary.

text: Triggers and symptom patterns: Environmental or activity-related triggers, individual differences and symptom diaries.
Which statement about asthma triggers is correct?
option_A: Everyone with asthma has exactly the same triggers
option_B: Triggers only occur indoors
option_C: Triggers never change across environments
option_D: Pollen may trigger asthma symptoms in some people
explanation_or_correction: Allergens such as pollen or dust mites are common triggers for some people.

text: Why can an asthma trigger diary be useful?
option_A: It shows patterns between exposures and symptoms to discuss with a clinician
option_B: It guarantees that no future symptoms will occur
option_C: It replaces all breathing tests
option_D: It establishes a diagnosis without a clinician
explanation_or_correction: A diary may reveal patterns, although it cannot by itself establish a cause or diagnosis.

text: Which statement about triggers is most accurate?
option_A: Only one trigger can ever exist
option_B: Triggers vary between individuals, so patterns and environments matter
option_C: Asthma symptoms can never be triggered by exercise
option_D: Every person with asthma responds to identical triggers
explanation_or_correction: Different people can have different triggers, including allergens, irritants and exercise.

text: Everyone with asthma has exactly the same triggers.
explanation_or_correction: Asthma triggers can differ between people; tracking personal patterns can help identify them.

text: Clinical assessment and monitoring: The role of symptom history and breathing tests in clinical evaluation; tracking changes over time.
Which statement about evaluating possible asthma is accurate?
option_A: A classroom quiz alone confirms asthma
option_B: A single symptom always confirms asthma by itself
option_C: Clinicians consider symptom history and appropriate breathing tests
option_D: Shoe size is sufficient for diagnosis
explanation_or_correction: Symptoms over time and objective breathing assessments may help evaluate asthma.

text: Why can recording symptom frequency be helpful?
option_A: It proves the exact cause without a clinician
option_B: It prevents all flare-ups
option_C: It replaces every clinician visit
option_D: It informs discussion about asthma control over time
explanation_or_correction: Symptom patterns and frequency can help clinicians review control.

text: Why is one isolated symptom not enough to determine a diagnosis?
option_A: Many different conditions can produce similar symptoms
option_B: Only wheezing counts as evidence
option_C: Symptoms are never relevant
option_D: A patient must always have every asthma symptom
explanation_or_correction: A healthcare professional considers patterns and appropriate tests because symptoms can overlap across conditions.

text: Asthma can always be confirmed from a single symptom alone.
explanation_or_correction: A healthcare professional considers symptom patterns and may use breathing tests to assess asthma.

text: General control and action planning: Differences between routine control and short-term symptom relief; following an individual asthma action plan.
Which statement about an asthma action plan is correct?
option_A: Once symptoms improve, the agreed asthma action plan is unnecessary
option_B: It gives individualized guidance about routine care and worsening symptoms
option_C: It is only useful after hospitalization
option_D: It is written by answering a classroom quiz
explanation_or_correction: An individualized plan helps the person recognize and respond to changes in asthma symptoms.

text: Why may some asthma treatments be used regularly even when someone feels well?
option_A: Only taking medicine during every school class works
option_B: Feeling well proves asthma cannot return
option_C: Some prescribed treatments help maintain control of airway inflammation
option_D: Regular treatment is never needed
explanation_or_correction: Long-term control treatment can be prescribed to reduce inflammation and prevent symptoms.

text: What is the safest general response before changing a prescribed asthma treatment?
option_A: Use someone else's inhaler
option_B: Follow instructions from a social media poll
option_C: Stop all medications whenever symptoms improve
option_D: Discuss the change with the treating clinician and follow the action plan
explanation_or_correction: Prescribed treatment should be adjusted with appropriate clinical guidance.

text: If symptoms improve, the individual asthma action plan is no longer needed.
explanation_or_correction: Ongoing management and treatment changes should follow the individual's agreed asthma action plan and clinical advice.

text: Migraine
explanation_or_correction: Draft educational reference: MedlinePlus, https://medlineplus.gov/migraine.html. Review scope, clinical red flags and teaching level with Lavin.

text: Migraine features: Migraine as a neurological headache disorder; common features and differences in symptom patterns.
Which statement best describes migraine?
option_A: It only affects the jaw joint
option_B: Migraine is always the same as a short, mild tension headache
option_C: It is a headache disorder that may include nausea and sensitivity to light or sound
option_D: It is caused only by a head injury
explanation_or_correction: Migraine is a neurological headache disorder with associated symptoms that differ by person.

text: Which symptom may accompany migraine headache?
option_A: Hair colour changes
option_B: Permanent loss of fingerprints
option_C: A broken ankle
option_D: Light sensitivity
explanation_or_correction: Sensitivity to light or sound and nausea can accompany migraine.

text: Why is it inaccurate to judge migraine only by how much head pain a person reports?
option_A: Migraine can have associated symptoms and variable patterns
option_B: Pain is never present during migraine
option_C: Only one pain intensity is possible
option_D: All migraines require hospitalization
explanation_or_correction: Migraine experiences vary, and related symptoms may be important.

text: A migraine is always the same as a short, mild tension headache.
explanation_or_correction: Migraine can involve more than head pain and can have distinctive symptoms such as nausea and sensitivity to light or sound.

text: Aura and accompanying symptoms: Recognizing aura, light/sound sensitivity and nausea as possible but not universal features.
Which statement about migraine aura is correct?
option_A: Every person with migraine must experience aura
option_B: Some migraines include temporary neurological symptoms called aura
option_C: Aura is a type of skin infection
option_D: Aura is the name of a pain medicine
explanation_or_correction: Aura may involve temporary visual or other neurological symptoms before or during some migraines.

text: Which statement about migraine with aura is accurate?
option_A: Every migraine must include aura
option_B: Aura proves a migraine diagnosis without assessment
option_C: Some people experience aura, and some do not
option_D: Aura only occurs after a week of pain
explanation_or_correction: Migraine may occur with or without aura.

text: Why should someone discuss new visual or neurological symptoms with a clinician?
option_A: All visual changes are harmless migraines
option_B: A student quiz can always diagnose aura
option_C: Such symptoms cannot occur outside migraine
option_D: Similar symptoms can have more than one cause and may need assessment
explanation_or_correction: New or unusual neurological symptoms should not be assumed to be migraine without appropriate evaluation.

text: Every person with migraine must experience aura.
explanation_or_correction: Some people have migraine with aura, while others have migraine without aura.

text: Triggers and symptom diaries: Individual trigger patterns and recording symptoms without assuming causation.
What is one purpose of a headache diary?
option_A: To record possible patterns, timing and symptoms
option_B: To replace professional assessment
option_C: To guarantee that migraines stop
option_D: To prove a specific food caused every headache
explanation_or_correction: A diary can help describe patterns for discussion with a care team, but does not prove cause.

text: Which statement about migraine triggers is most accurate?
option_A: Triggers cannot vary by context
option_B: Possible triggers differ across people, and patterns may be worth discussing
option_C: A single event proves a trigger for life
option_D: Everyone has identical triggers
explanation_or_correction: Triggers and symptom patterns vary between people.

text: Why should a student avoid claiming a trigger from one diary entry?
option_A: A diary contains clinical laboratory tests
option_B: Triggers can be established from handwriting style
option_C: One event cannot establish causality, even if symptoms happened afterward
option_D: Temporal order is always proof of causation
explanation_or_correction: An isolated association is not enough to establish a cause.

text: A diary entry proves that one particular food caused a migraine.
explanation_or_correction: A diary can identify possible patterns, but temporal association alone does not prove causation.

text: Clinical evaluation and warning changes: The value of professional assessment for new, unusual or changing headaches.
Which statement about changing headache symptoms is most appropriate?
option_A: A sudden major change in headache pattern never needs assessment

option_D: A new or noticeably changing headache pattern deserves clinical assessment
explanation_or_correction: New, unusual or changing headaches may need clinical assessment.

text: Why does a clinician ask about the timing and associated symptoms of headache?
option_A: To distinguish possible causes and understand a person's pattern
option_B: To determine hair colour
option_C: To avoid asking about symptoms
option_D: To replace any appropriate examination

option_A: Medical advice and the individual's existing plan

text: Pneumonia and the lungs: An infection that can inflame the air sacs in the lungs and affect breathing.
Which organ is mainly affected by pneumonia?
option_A: The throat alone, never the lungs
option_B: The stomach
option_C: The outer ear
option_D: The lungs
explanation_or_correction: Pneumonia is an infection in one or both lungs that affects air sacs.

text: What may happen to lung air sacs during pneumonia?
option_A: They may become inflamed and fill with fluid or pus
option_B: They cease to exist permanently
option_C: They produce hair
option_D: They transform into bone
explanation_or_correction: Pneumonia can cause air sac inflammation and fluid accumulation, which may impair breathing.

text: Why can pneumonia make breathing harder?
option_A: The lungs stop needing oxygen
option_B: Inflammation and fluid in lung air sacs can interfere with gas exchange
option_C: Pneumonia changes only the colour of blood
option_D: Air sacs carry food to the stomach
explanation_or_correction: Inflamed or fluid-filled air sacs can make oxygen exchange more difficult.

text: Pneumonia affects only the throat, not the lungs.
explanation_or_correction: Pneumonia is a lung infection that may inflame and fill air sacs with fluid or pus.

text: Symptoms and patient assessment: Common respiratory and systemic symptoms and the need for clinical assessment when appropriate.
Which statement about pneumonia symptoms is accurate?
option_A: Symptoms can never change with the cause
option_B: Symptoms only change a person's hair colour
option_C: Cough, fever or breathing difficulty may occur
option_D: Every person with pneumonia has exactly the same symptoms
explanation_or_correction: Cough, fever, breathing difficulty and other symptoms may occur.

text: Why can pneumonia symptoms look different between patients?
option_A: All patients must have identical symptoms
option_B: Symptoms never depend on underlying health
option_C: Any cough alone proves pneumonia
option_D: Symptoms may vary with the cause, age and other health factors
explanation_or_correction: The presentation may differ among patients, so clinical context matters.

text: Why might a clinician examine someone with cough, fever and difficulty breathing?
option_A: To assess potential causes and whether further investigation is needed
option_B: To diagnose pneumonia from favourite foods
option_C: To replace medical examination with a school quiz
option_D: Because these symptoms always rule out infection
explanation_or_correction: Clinical assessment helps distinguish causes and guide appropriate evaluation.

text: Pneumonia always causes exactly the same symptoms in every person.
explanation_or_correction: Symptoms can vary with the person and cause; cough, fever and breathing difficulty are possible.

text: Causes and spread: Different infectious causes and the difference between a cause and a person's individual diagnosis.
Which statement about pneumonia causes is accurate?
option_A: Only cold weather directly causes pneumonia
option_B: Bacteria and viruses are among the organisms that can cause pneumonia
option_C: Every pneumonia is caused by pollen
option_D: Every pneumonia is bacterial and needs the same antibiotic
explanation_or_correction: Pneumonia may have different infectious causes, including bacterial and viral infections.

text: Why does distinguishing the likely cause of pneumonia matter?
option_A: It makes every antibiotic appropriate
option_B: The cause cannot influence treatment
option_C: Different causes may require different care decisions
option_D: The cause always changes a person's blood type
explanation_or_correction: Cause and clinical severity help guide assessment and care.

text: What can students correctly infer from a case description of cough and fever?
option_A: No clinical review is necessary
option_B: The cause is definitely bacterial
option_C: The cause is definitely viral
option_D: Symptoms alone may not establish the exact organism or diagnosis
explanation_or_correction: Symptoms alone may not distinguish different infectious causes.

text: Every pneumonia infection is caused by bacteria and always needs the same antibiotic.
explanation_or_correction: Different organisms, including bacteria and viruses, can cause pneumonia; treatment depends on a clinical assessment.

text: Treatment decisions and warning symptoms: The role of clinician assessment, cause-dependent treatment and recognition of worsening breathing.
What is a safe general approach to choosing treatment for possible pneumonia?
option_A: Seek appropriate clinical assessment because treatment depends on cause and severity
option_B: Use someone else's prescription
option_C: Always choose identical antibiotics
option_D: Select a medicine based only on a school multiple-choice test
explanation_or_correction: Treatment decisions must reflect a qualified healthcare professional's evaluation.

text: Which worsening symptom should prompt timely medical attention?
option_A: A different favourite song
option_B: Increasing difficulty breathing
option_C: A preference for a different study notebook
option_D: Changing a phone wallpaper
explanation_or_correction: Worsening breathing can be serious and should prompt timely medical attention.

text: Why is an educational question insufficient to prescribe pneumonia treatment?
option_A: Medication choices depend only on classroom quiz scores
option_B: All pneumonias are harmless
option_C: The cause, severity, individual health conditions and clinical examination affect decisions
option_D: Every person has the same clinical circumstances
explanation_or_correction: Individual diagnosis and prescribing require clinical evaluation.

text: Every person with pneumonia should choose medicine from an online questionnaire.
explanation_or_correction: Assessment and treatment choices should be made by a healthcare professional, especially with worsening breathing.

text: Prevention and recovery: General prevention measures, vaccination discussions, recovery and follow-up.
Which action may help reduce some risks of pneumonia?
option_A: Sharing personal medications

explanation_or_correction: Vaccinations and hygiene can reduce some causes and transmission risks.

text: Why might follow-up matter during recovery from pneumonia?
option_A: Symptoms and recovery vary, and persistent or worsening problems need assessment
option_B: All people recover within the same exact time
option_C: Once fever ends, all complications are impossible
option_D: No one should discuss new symptoms
explanation_or_correction: Recovery can vary; persistent or worsening symptoms deserve follow-up.

text: Which statement best describes pneumonia prevention?
option_A: Vaccination is irrelevant for all respiratory infections
option_B: A combination of appropriate preventive measures can reduce risk but cannot guarantee prevention
option_C: Every case is prevented by antibiotics
option_D: Only one measure is needed to eliminate every cause
explanation_or_correction: Prevention depends on cause and risk factors, and no single measure removes all risk.

text: Pneumonia prevention consists of one measure that eliminates all risk.
explanation_or_correction: Prevention can involve recommended vaccinations, hygiene and other individual risk-reduction measures; no single measure prevents every infection.
